explain.say: An earthworm has no legs and no bones, yet it crawls and burrows through soil. It uses a fluid-filled body, two sets of muscles and tiny bristles, in a cycle that repeats again and again.

faq.q: How do earthworms move without bones?
faq.a: An earthworm uses its fluid-filled body as a skeleton. Ring muscles squeeze segments long and thin, long muscles pull them short and fat, and bristles grip the soil so these changes in shape push it along.

faq.q: What are the bristles on a worm for?
faq.a: The bristles, called setae, are tiny hairs on each segment. They poke out to grip the soil so part of the worm stays anchored while another part moves, a bit like the spikes on running shoes.

A hydrostatic skeleton is a body held in shape by fluid under pressure, like a water balloon. Muscles squeeze the fluid to change the body's shape, which is how worms, jellyfish and sea anemones move.

faq.q: Why do worms come out when it rains?
faq.a: Scientists are not completely sure. Worms breathe through moist skin, and rain lets them travel across the surface without drying out; the drumming of rain may also make them come up.
asks: Why are worms on the path after rain?
Do worms drown in the rain?

faq.a: Yes. By sending the wave of muscle contractions the other way and switching which bristles grip, an earthworm can back out of its burrow.
